title: Lecture 1: Introduction to the Chinese Financial System

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Hey, welcome back. So, this is the first episode for Financial Markets and Investments in China. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And I'm Leo. And, uh, full honesty, when I opened this first lecture I thought, okay, intro week, definitions, easy.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And then there's like... twenty six slides of classifications.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah, it's a lot of boxes. But here's the thing. This lecture is basically the map for the whole course. The professor literally says that on the last slide. Authorities on top, markets and institutions underneath. Everything later hangs on this.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, so let's build the map. Where do we start?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We start with the simplest question. What is finance, actually?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Money. Next question.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Ha. Close. The lecture defines it as the flow of funds between different sectors of the economy. And the key idea is that some sectors have more money than they spend, and some have less.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Surplus and shortage.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. Surplus sectors, that's usually households. You earn your salary, you don't spend all of it, you save. And shortage sectors, usually firms and the government. They want to build a factory, a railway, whatever, and they need more money than they have.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So finance is the plumbing that moves money from my savings account to someone's factory.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's a really good way to put it. And there are two ways the plumbing works. One is fiscal. The government taxes the surplus and spends it. The other is financial. Banks and markets link the two sides.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And within the financial way, there's direct and indirect, right?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes. Direct finance is when you, the saver, give money straight to the borrower. You buy a company's stock, you buy a government bond. No middleman owns that claim.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And indirect is the bank.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Indirect is the bank. You deposit money, the bank lends it out. You never meet the borrower. You have a claim on the bank, and the bank has a claim on the borrower.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, and there's this line on the slide I liked. Markets and intermediaries are complements, not substitutes.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah, that one's worth remembering. Markets price and trade claims. Intermediaries pool, transform and monitor risk. You need both. Which, honestly, matters a lot for China, because China is very bank heavy. We'll see that in later lectures.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Alright. Then we get into assets. And this is where I started to glaze over a bit, I'll admit.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Let me try to make it painless. An asset is anything that's valuable in exchange. Tangible assets are physical, like land or a machine. Intangible ones have no physical form, like a patent, a brand, goodwill. And financial assets.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Which are?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: A claim. A financial asset entitles you to receive cash, or another financial asset, from somebody else. And the slide makes a sharp point here. Unlike a real asset, its value depends on the issuer's ability and willingness to pay.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So a bond is only worth something if the company can actually pay me back.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. A house is still a house even if the builder goes bankrupt. A bond from a bankrupt company is, well...

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Wallpaper.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Pretty much. Then there's this trio that I think is actually the most useful thing in the first half. Instruments, assets and products.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, I'll be honest, I thought those were synonyms.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Most people do. The trick is it's the same thing seen from three angles. Take one corporate bond. To the company that issued it, it's an instrument, a legal contract they used to raise money. To you, the person holding it, it's an asset on your balance sheet. And when a bank packages a bunch of those bonds into a fund and sells it to the public, that's a product.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Oh, that's neat. Issuer view, holder view, market view.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. One security, three identities.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And products are, what, standardized?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's the key word. A product is a standardized offering. Think mutual funds, ETFs, insurance policies, structured deposits. And standardization matters for three reasons. Contracts are uniform, so you can compare them. Pricing is transparent. And because they're all the same, they can trade easily in a secondary market.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Like a Treasury bond. Every one has the same maturity, coupon, face value.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly the example in the slides.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay. Then we classify instruments. By duration and by nature.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: By duration is the money market versus the capital market. Under one year is money market. Treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit. Over one year is capital market. Stocks, bonds, mortgages.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And by nature, debt, equity, derivatives.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Debt is a fixed claim. You lent money, you get your interest and principal back, nothing more. Equity is a residual claim. You own a piece, you get whatever's left after everyone else is paid. Could be a lot, could be zero.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And derivatives are the weird ones.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Derivatives are contracts whose payoff depends on something else. A stock, an interest rate, oil, a currency. Futures, options, swaps.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay. That's the asset side. Now markets.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So a financial market is a platform where buyers and sellers trade financial assets. And the lecture lists five functions. Want to try?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Hmm. Moving savings into investment.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Liquidity. Being able to sell when you want.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Price discovery?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yep. Prices reflect supply, demand, and information.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Uh... reducing costs?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Transaction costs, yes. And the fifth one is risk. Markets let you transfer, hedge, and diversify risk.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Four out of five, I'll take it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Then there's this long section on six ways to classify markets. I'll go fast, because honestly, this is the kind of thing you'll want to look at in the summary tab rather than hear.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Good call.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: By what's traded. Money market, capital market, foreign exchange, gold. By financing method, direct or indirect. By transaction level, primary or secondary.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Primary is when the security is first issued. Like an IPO.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. The company gets the money. Secondary is when investors trade it among themselves afterwards. The company doesn't get anything from that, but it's what gives investors liquidity. And honestly, without a good secondary market, nobody would buy in the primary one.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Because you'd be stuck with it forever.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. Then by pricing, open market with public bidding, like a stock exchange, versus negotiated, like over the counter. By organization, visible markets with a central venue versus invisible ones, dealer networks, like the FX market. And by delivery timing, spot versus derivatives.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay. And then China specifically.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: China today has the full set. Money market, bond market, stock market, foreign exchange, commodity futures, financial derivatives, venture capital and private equity, insurance and funds, and a gold market.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: I want to flag one thing from the money market slide. Repos. Repurchase agreements. Those come up again, right?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Oh, a lot. Especially in the monetary policy lecture. A repo is basically a short, collateralized loan. I sell you a bond today and promise to buy it back tomorrow at a slightly higher price. That small difference is the interest rate. Banks do this with each other, and with the central bank, all day long.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Got it. And for the capital market, the slide says in China the two pillars are equities and long term bonds.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes. And then FX, which is the biggest and most liquid market in the world, trading twenty four hours. And derivatives, where the slide makes a nice distinction. Over the counter derivatives are bigger but less regulated. Exchange traded ones are more transparent.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And four functions for derivatives. Hedging, speculation, price discovery, arbitrage.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: You were paying attention.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: I had coffee.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Okay, last big block. Institutions. And this is where China starts to look different.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Two classes. Regulators and intermediaries.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. The regulators first. The People's Bank of China, the PBOC, is the central bank. Monetary policy. The CSRC, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, handles stocks, bonds, futures. And the NFRA, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, handles banking and insurance.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And SAFE.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: SAFE, the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, runs FX, the reserves, and capital account rules. And it's administered by the PBOC. And then, since twenty twenty three, there's the Central Financial Commission sitting above all of them, at the Party level, coordinating.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the Ministry of Finance owns the big banks' capital through something called Central Huijin.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. Which tells you something. In China, the state is not just the referee. It's also the main shareholder.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, intermediaries. The slide says China's system is built around large state owned commercial banks, with lots of other institutions around them.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And then there's a line about the central bank I really like. A commercial bank's liability is a deposit you hold. The central bank's liability is the currency everyone holds. That difference is why it can set the price of money.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Ooh. Say that again?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: When you hold a hundred yuan note, that's technically a liability of the central bank. Everyone uses it. So the central bank decides how much of the base money exists and what it costs. A normal bank can't do that.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: That's a good one for the exam. Okay, and policy banks?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Policy banks are state banks that lend for national goals, not profit. Infrastructure, exports, agriculture. They don't take public deposits; they fund themselves with state capital and bonds.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And commercial banks create money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes, and that surprises people. When a bank makes a loan, it credits the borrower's account. That's a brand new deposit. So lending literally expands the money supply.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, then the non banks. Eight of them. Let me try to do this quickly. Securities companies.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Investment banks, basically. Brokerage, trading, underwriting IPOs. Fun fact from the slide, in the US they're called investment banks, in East Asia securities firms, and in Germany they're often just a division of a universal bank.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Fund management companies.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Pool money from lots of people, professional managers invest it. The slide calls it risk sharing by contract. The direct finance idea wearing an intermediary's clothes.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Ha, nice. Stock exchanges.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Three of them. Shanghai, nineteen ninety. Shenzhen, also nineteen ninety, known for growth and tech. And Beijing, twenty twenty one, for innovative small and medium firms. And they're legally not for profit, self regulating.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Then asset management companies. The AMCs.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: These are interesting. Four big ones were created in the late nineties to take bad loans, non performing loans, off the books of the state banks. Basically a cleanup crew. And the slide adds, they are also balance sheets that can fail like any other.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Which, I think one of them did get into trouble a few years back.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah, let's not go there today, but keep that in mind. Insurance companies. Two sided business. They collect premiums and pay claims, and in the meantime they invest those premiums, so they're huge institutional investors.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Trust companies.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: This is the one with the honest footnote. Officially, trusts manage assets for clients and don't take deposits. But in practice, the slide says, pooled trust plans long served as a deposit substitute with implicit guarantees.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Meaning people thought they were as safe as a bank deposit.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. Hold onto that. It's basically shadow banking, which comes back later.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And then leasing companies, and finance companies, which are like internal banks for big corporate groups.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. And to wrap the section, seven functions of intermediaries. The ones I'd really remember are information production, they screen and monitor borrowers, and maturity transformation.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Borrow short, lend long.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. Your deposit can be withdrawn tomorrow, but the bank uses it to fund a twenty year mortgage. That's the magic, and also the fragility, of banking.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay. So if you had to compress this whole lecture into, like, three things to remember?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: One. Finance moves money from surplus sectors, mostly households, to shortage sectors, mostly firms and government, either directly through markets or indirectly through banks. Two. The same security is an instrument, an asset, and a product depending on who's looking. And three. China's system is a map with authorities on top, the PBOC, the CSRC, the NFRA, SAFE, coordinated by the Central Financial Commission, and markets and institutions underneath, with big state banks at the center.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Perfect. And next time, the history. How China went from a planned economy to all of this.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Which is honestly the fun part. See you then.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: See you.
